summary: An early 1969 memo on functional specifications for the ARPA Network. It belongs to the first wave of notes in which the Network Working Group worked out what the network should do and how connected computers would use it. It is a planning document rather than a finished specification.

plainLanguage.summary: Before building the network, people wrote down what it should be able to do, like listing the rules and features of a new game before making it.

questions: what was link 0 in the early arpanet
how did early arpanet hosts check transmissions
subtitle: A handwritten May 1969 specification covering error checks, host-to-host links, and how two hosts open a connection.

tldr.problem: Hosts on the planned ARPA network needed an agreed picture of how to check transmissions, how many logical links they share, and what software each host must provide.
tldr.mechanism: The note defines a host-to-host checksum, describes a control link and teletype-like and file-like links, divides host software into a user program, a network program and a transmission handler, and walks through opening a link from UCLA to SRI.
tldr.outcome: It is an early working note rather than a finished standard, and later notes revise its details; RFC 9 by the same author, for example, counts 256 logical links where this note counts 32.

today: The unit metadata records the status of RFC 8 as Unknown and lists no obsoleting or updating RFC. It is an early planning note from May 1969, and its link count differs from the later RFC RFC 9 by the same author.

sections.title: Transmission Checking
sections.content:
The note names two kinds of transmission checking. Between IMPs, a cyclic checksum is computed and checked by the BBN hardware. Between hosts, a special 16-bit checksum is computed and checked by the host programs.

For the host checksum a message is broken into 1152-bit pieces, an end-around carry sum is calculated for each piece, and the pieces are combined with increasing weights (the sum of the first piece, plus twice the sum of the second, plus four times the sum of the third, and so on). The 16-bit result sits just after the marking of the host heading. The author says this also guards against bad host-to-IMP or IMP-to-host transmission and against IMP packet number inversion, and gives a small worked end-around carry example.
sections.plainLanguage: It is like counting the pieces in a puzzle box twice, once when it is packed and once when it arrives, to check nothing fell out.

sections.title: Links Between Two Hosts
sections.content:
Thirty-two links are possible between two hosts, and each is viewed as full duplex. Link 0 is a control link, used for connection requests and status of any kind. The other 31 serve either as teletype-like connections or as file transmission connections.

A teletype-like connection carries ASCII characters, the remote host generates the echoes and looks for break or interrupt control characters, and the transmission is slow.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of 32 phone lines between two houses. One is only for saying who is going to call whom, and the rest carry chats or big deliveries.

sections.title: Functional Software Specifications
sections.content:
The note splits host software into three parts. The user program is an application such as the NLS program at SRI. It is viewed as a local control part (the user interface) and a hard part (the application), and the local control program could be sent to another host, written in a Decode Encode Language called DEL, so that only program data crosses the link.

The network program multiplexes outgoing messages and distributes incoming ones, runs link initiation, builds the host message heading, computes and checks the host-host checksum, receives RFNM control messages and supervises the handler. The transmission handler is initiated by the network program or by the I/O interrupt, controls the channel hardware unit and is very short.
sections.plainLanguage: There is a person who does the job, a manager who sorts the mail and checks it, and a small driver who runs the van.

sections.title: Establishing a Link
sections.content:
The general procedure is to establish a teletype-like link to the remote host in a pre-log-in state, send and receive characters, then set up a file-like link in parallel, which both host user programs must do, and send over it.

In the example, a user at UCLA wants NLS at SRI. The network program selects an open link, for example 25, sends a message over link 0 requesting a connection on link 25, and waits for an acceptance over link 0. If both sides try the same link at once, the one with the higher priority prevails; the author suggests priority be exactly the host identification number.
sections.plainLanguage: You first ring the front desk line to ask for a room number, wait for a yes, then use that room. If two people ask for the same room at once, the one with the higher number wins.
